scene-u01-pnew3-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew3-25.text: Symbols: meet the six symbols first

scene-u01-pnew3-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew3-26.text: Indices start at 0; in 1-D $d,f$ are the $M,k$ of KP05.

scene-u01-pnew3-44.name: text#44
scene-u01-pnew3-44.text: input channels, output channels (= number of kernels)

scene-u01-pnew3-49.name: text#49
scene-u01-pnew3-49.text: These six symbols are all you need to remember.

scene-u01-pnew4-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew4-25.text: The kernel must lie completely inside the input to count

scene-u01-pnew4-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew4-26.text: Input $d=8$, kernel $f=3$: where can the top-left corner of the kernel stand?

scene-u01-pnew4-61.name: text#61
scene-u01-pnew4-61.text: the last position is $d-f=5$; further right the kernel sticks out

scene-u01-pnew4-63.name: text#63
scene-u01-pnew4-63.text: number of positions $=d-f+1=6$, so the output side is $6$

scene-u01-pnew4-65.name: text#65
scene-u01-pnew4-65.text: Without padding the output side is $d-f+1$.

scene-u01-pnew5-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew5-25.text: In 2-D: $5\times5$ with a $3\times3$ kernel gives a $3\times3$ output

scene-u01-pnew5-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew5-26.text: The kernel's centre can never stand on the outermost ring.

scene-u01-pnew5-107.name: text#107
scene-u01-pnew5-107.text:
output $3\times3=9$ cells
$5\times5$ shrank by a ring

scene-u01-pnew5-109.name: text#109
scene-u01-pnew5-109.text: Only $3\times3$ positions keep the kernel inside the input.

scene-u01-pnew6-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew6-25.text: Stack many layers and each shrinks by a ring: the image soon gets small

scene-u01-pnew6-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew6-26.text: Every layer reduces the side by $f-1=2$ ($f=3$, no padding).

scene-u01-pnew6-38.name: text#38
scene-u01-pnew6-38.text: $5\to3\to1$: two layers and it is gone

scene-u01-pnew6-51.name: text#51
scene-u01-pnew6-51.text: a $224\times224$ image through repeated $3\times3$ valid convolutions

scene-u01-pnew6-81.name: text#81
scene-u01-pnew6-81.text: With more layers the border is cut away again and again!

scene-u01-pnew6-83.name: text#83
scene-u01-pnew6-83.text: The remedy: pad a few rings of cells around the input before convolving.

scene-u01-pnew7-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew7-25.text: Padding: add $p$ rings of cells around the input

scene-u01-pnew7-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew7-26.text: Padding $p$ rings per side makes the input side $d+2p$.

scene-u01-pnew7-113.name: text#113
scene-u01-pnew7-113.text: Pad one ring and the ring that was cut off is given back.

scene-u01-pnew8-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew8-26.text: No padding ($p=0$) is valid; padding until the output is as large as the input is same.

scene-u01-pnew8-59.name: text#59
scene-u01-pnew8-59.text: $5\to3$: the outer ring is cut off

scene-u01-pnew8-118.name: text#118
scene-u01-pnew8-118.text: valid only means "no extension, compute inside the original signal"

scene-u01-pnew8-120.name: text#120
scene-u01-pnew8-120.text: Common misconception: valid is not the "more correct" padding.

scene-u01-pnew9-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew9-25.text: Stride $s$: how many cells the kernel moves at a time

scene-u01-pnew9-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew9-26.text: Until now $s=1$; with $s=2$ an output is computed only every second cell.

scene-u01-pnew9-55.name: text#55
scene-u01-pnew9-55.text:
only positions $0,2,4$ give outputs
$3$ outputs ($6$ when $s=1$)

scene-u01-pnew9-57.name: text#57
scene-u01-pnew9-57.text: The larger the stride, the farther the kernel moves and the fewer the outputs.

scene-u01-pnew10-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew10-25.text: The number of positions: the formula in three steps

scene-u01-pnew10-31.name: text#31
scene-u01-pnew10-31.text:
the farthest the kernel can go
$d-f+2p$

scene-u01-pnew10-44.name: text#44
scene-u01-pnew10-44.text: The number of steps, plus the position where the kernel started.

scene-u01-pnew11-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew11-25.text: Four examples: see how the windows lie

scene-u01-pnew11-119.name: text#119
scene-u01-pnew11-119.text: The same input, different strides: different numbers of outputs and unread cells.

scene-u01-pnew12-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew12-25.text: The consequence of rounding: some cells are never read

scene-u01-pnew12-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew12-26.text: $d=8,\ f=3,\ s=2$: the final leftover is less than one step.

scene-u01-pnew12-85.name: text#85
scene-u01-pnew12-85.text: Nobody looks at the last cell!

scene-u01-pnew12-87.name: text#87
scene-u01-pnew12-87.text: we round down since the kernel moves in whole steps: a leftover under one step is dropped

scene-u01-pnew12-89.name: text#89
scene-u01-pnew12-89.text: common error: thinking the rounding is a minor detail

scene-u01-pnew12-91.name: text#91
scene-u01-pnew12-91.text: Rounding = cells at the right (and bottom) of the input may never be read.

scene-u01-pnew13-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew13-25.text: Two side effects of a stride larger than 1

scene-u01-pnew13-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew13-26.text: One: the output gets smaller; two: translation equivariance weakens (KP06).

scene-u01-pnew13-37.name: text#37
scene-u01-pnew13-37.text:
KP06: a convolution with stride $s$
is equivariant only to multiples of $s$

scene-u01-pnew13-40.name: text#40
scene-u01-pnew13-40.text: so a stride of $2$ is a way to shrink on the way, with the price that comes with it

scene-u01-pnew13-42.name: text#42
scene-u01-pnew13-42.text: Stride: a smaller output, at the price of part of the equivariance.

scene-u01-pnew14-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew14-25.text: What numbers fill the padded cells?

scene-u01-pnew14-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew14-26.text: Zero is the most common, and there are four more.

scene-u01-pnew14-54.name: text#54
scene-u01-pnew14-54.text: Five methods: zero, constant, replicate, reflect, circular.

scene-u01-pnew15-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew15-26.text: The simplest rule: fill both ends with the same number.

scene-u01-pnew15-65.name: text#65
scene-u01-pnew15-65.text: zero is simplest and most common; a constant can set a background value

scene-u01-pnew15-67.name: text#67
scene-u01-pnew15-67.text: Zero padding creates an artificial dark ring at the border.

scene-u01-pnew16-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew16-25.text: Replicate, reflect, circular: where the padded values come from

scene-u01-pnew16-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew16-26.text: Every padded cell has a source it copies from.

scene-u01-pnew16-69.name: text#69
scene-u01-pnew16-69.text: circular: take from the other end

scene-u01-pnew16-88.name: text#88
scene-u01-pnew16-88.text: The same one ring: replicate $[3,\ldots,2]$, reflect $[1,\ldots,4]$, circular $[2,\ldots,3]$.

scene-u01-pnew17-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew17-25.text: How to choose? See whether the padded values look like a real image

scene-u01-pnew17-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew17-26.text: The source lists common uses of each method; this note has not checked them one by one.

scene-u01-pnew17-33.name: text#33
scene-u01-pnew17-33.text: an artificial dark ring at the border

scene-u01-pnew17-37.name: text#37
scene-u01-pnew17-37.text: the pattern at the border continues

scene-u01-pnew17-41.name: text#41
scene-u01-pnew17-41.text: suits data whose ends really join (such as a wrap-around panorama)

scene-u01-pnew17-45.name: text#45
scene-u01-pnew17-45.text: can set a background value (such as mean brightness)

scene-u01-pnew17-47.name: text#47
scene-u01-pnew17-47.text: look at the nature of the data first; do not copy only because others use it

scene-u01-pnew17-49.name: text#49
scene-u01-pnew17-49.text: There is no single correct padding: look at the data.

scene-u01-pnew18-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew18-25.text: How many rings does same need?

scene-u01-pnew18-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew18-26.text: Take stride $s=1$ and require the output side to equal $d$.

scene-u01-pnew18-177.name: text#177
scene-u01-pnew18-177.text: Odd kernel side and stride $1$: pad $\frac{f-1}{2}$ rings and you get same.

scene-u01-pnew19-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew19-25.text: Same does not always keep the size

scene-u01-pnew19-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew19-26.text: The formula has conditions: $s=1$ and $f$ odd.

scene-u01-pnew19-38.name: text#38
scene-u01-pnew19-38.text: not $224$: the padding did not keep the size

scene-u01-pnew19-42.name: text#42
scene-u01-pnew19-42.text:
$p=\dfrac{4-1}{2}=1.5$
not a whole number of rings

scene-u01-pnew19-45.name: text#45
scene-u01-pnew19-45.text: an even kernel has no exact same (the two sides need different numbers of rings)

scene-u01-pnew19-47.name: text#47
scene-u01-pnew19-47.text: Common error: believing that "same padding" always keeps the size.

scene-u01-pnew20-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew20-25.text: A colour image: three planes stacked together

scene-u01-pnew20-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew20-26.text: Each pixel has red, green, blue numbers → three channels.

scene-u01-pnew20-38.name: text#38
scene-u01-pnew20-38.text: every channel is a $d\times d$ plane

scene-u01-pnew20-62.name: text#62
scene-u01-pnew20-62.text: In general the input has $C_{\mathrm{in}}$ channels.

scene-u01-pnew20-64.name: text#64
scene-u01-pnew20-64.text: Channels = maps stacked together; a grayscale image has only $1$.

scene-u01-pnew21-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew21-25.text: A kernel needs depth too: one slice per channel

scene-u01-pnew21-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew21-26.text: The size of the kernel is $f\times f\times C_{\mathrm{in}}$.

scene-u01-pnew21-46.name: text#46
scene-u01-pnew21-46.text:
add the results of the 3 channels
→ one number

scene-u01-pnew21-50.name: text#50
scene-u01-pnew21-50.text:
so one kernel
produces one feature map

scene-u01-pnew21-52.name: text#52
scene-u01-pnew21-52.text: The depth of a kernel equals the number of input channels $C_{\mathrm{in}}$.

scene-u01-pnew22-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew22-26.text: Two $3\times3$ input channels; two kernels, each $2\times2\times2$; no padding, $s=1$.

scene-u01-pnew22-113.name: text#113
scene-u01-pnew22-113.text: Write down the input and the kernels first: the next page computes one output.

scene-u01-pnew23-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew23-25.text: Worked example (2): the output of kernel 0 at position (0,0)

scene-u01-pnew23-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew23-26.text: Each channel does one multiply-and-add, then add the results.

scene-u01-pnew23-31.name: text#31
scene-u01-pnew23-31.text: channel 0: top-left $2\times2$ with slice 0 of kernel 0

scene-u01-pnew23-55.name: text#55
scene-u01-pnew23-55.text: channel 1: top-left $2\times2$ with slice 1 of kernel 0

scene-u01-pnew23-84.name: text#84
scene-u01-pnew23-84.text: The multiply-add results of the channels are added to give one output.

scene-u01-pnew24-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew24-25.text: Worked example (3): two kernels, two feature maps

scene-u01-pnew24-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew24-26.text: Computing every position gives two $2\times2$ maps.

scene-u01-pnew24-51.name: text#51
scene-u01-pnew24-51.text:
2 kernels → 2 feature maps of $2\times2$
the output is $2\times2\times2$

scene-u01-pnew24-53.name: text#53
scene-u01-pnew24-53.text: Input $3\times3\times2$ → output $2\times2\times2$: the depth is set by the number of kernels.

scene-u01-pnew25-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew25-26.text: The two numbers are set by different things.

scene-u01-pnew25-35.name: text#35
scene-u01-pnew25-35.text: as many slices as the input has channels

scene-u01-pnew25-41.name: text#41
scene-u01-pnew25-41.text: as many kernels as the feature maps we want

scene-u01-pnew25-48.name: text#48
scene-u01-pnew25-48.text: The depth is set by the input; the number of maps by the number of kernels.

scene-u01-pnew26-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew26-25.text: Number of weights: $f\times f\times C_{\mathrm{in}}\times C_{\mathrm{out}}$, plus biases

scene-u01-pnew26-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew26-26.text: Every kernel has its own weights; kernels do not share with each other.

scene-u01-pnew26-42.name: text#42
scene-u01-pnew26-42.text: every kernel is a stack of $f\times f\times C_{\mathrm{in}}$

scene-u01-pnew26-44.name: text#44
scene-u01-pnew26-44.text: weights of one kernel: $f\times f\times C_{\mathrm{in}}$

scene-u01-pnew26-46.name: text#46
scene-u01-pnew26-46.text: biases: one per kernel, $C_{\mathrm{out}}$ in all (counted separately)

scene-u01-pnew27-26.text: First: how large is the output?

scene-u01-pnew28-25.text: Weights, parameters, multiply-adds: step by step

scene-u01-pnew28-37.name: text#37
scene-u01-pnew28-37.text: Only $1{,}728$ weights, yet about $8.7\times10^{7}$ multiply-adds (KP05: sharing saves weights only).

scene-u01-pnew29-25.name: text#25
scene-u01-pnew29-25.text: A fair comparison with a fully connected layer: same input, same output

scene-u01-pnew29-26.name: text#26
scene-u01-pnew29-26.text: KP01 said the sizes differ so do not divide; with padding the output is also $224\times224\times64$.

scene-u01-pnew29-40.name: text#40
scene-u01-pnew29-40.text:
fully connected: $150{,}528\times3{,}211{,}264$ weights
about $279{,}736{,}775$ times the convolution's

scene-u01-pnew29-42.name: text#42
scene-u01-pnew29-42.text: Sparse connectivity and sharing cut the weights of the same task by more than eight orders of magnitude.

scene-u01-pnew30-26.text: For a new layer, come back to this table first.

scene-u01-pnew30-37.name: text#37
scene-u01-pnew30-37.text: output side $+2p$ (gives back the cut rings)

scene-u01-pnew30-41.name: text#41
scene-u01-pnew30-41.text: output side about $\div s$; after rounding some cells may be unread

scene-u01-pnew30-45.name: text#45
scene-u01-pnew30-45.text: depth of the kernel; weights $\propto C_{\mathrm{in}}$

steps.label: KP07 · 1/36 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: The question: after one convolutional layer, how large is the feature map and how many weights? Four knobs decide it: the stride, the padding, the side of the kernel and the channels.

steps.label: KP07 · 1/36 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: After this note, given the four knobs you can compute the output and the weights on your own, without anyone explaining.

steps.label: KP07 · 6/36 (3)

steps.label: KP07 · 8/36 (1)

steps.label: KP07 · 8/36 (3)

steps.label: KP07 · 9/36

steps.label: KP07 · 9/36 (1)

steps.label: KP07 · 9/36 (2)

steps.label: KP07 · 9/36 (3)

steps.label: KP07 · 10/36
steps.speakerNotes: The formula comes in three steps. First: how far the kernel can go. The padded input has side d plus two p and the kernel takes f cells, so the farthest it can go is d minus f plus two p. In the example, eight minus three is five.

steps.label: KP07 · 10/36 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: The formula comes in three steps. First: how far the kernel can go. The padded input has side d plus two p and the kernel takes f cells, so the farthest it can go is d minus f plus two p. In the example, eight minus three is five.

steps.label: KP07 · 10/36 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Second: every step moves s cells and only whole steps are allowed, so the number of steps is that distance divided by s, rounded down. Five divided by two, rounded down, is two.

steps.label: KP07 · 10/36 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Third: the number of positions is the number of steps plus the position where the kernel started: two plus one equals three. Together: the output side equals d minus f plus two p, divided by s, rounded down, plus one.

steps.label: KP07 · 11/36
steps.speakerNotes: Fix a kernel of three cells and no padding. With d equal to eight and a stride of one there are six outputs and every cell is read. With d equal to eight and a stride of two there are three outputs and cell seven is never read.

steps.label: KP07 · 11/36 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Fix a kernel of three cells and no padding. With d equal to eight and a stride of one there are six outputs and every cell is read. With d equal to eight and a stride of two there are three outputs and cell seven is never read.

steps.label: KP07 · 11/36 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: With d equal to eight and a stride of three there are only two outputs and cells six and seven are never read.

steps.label: KP07 · 11/36 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: With d equal to seven and a stride of two there are three outputs, every cell is read, and no leftover. The same input with different strides gives different numbers of outputs and unread cells.

steps.label: KP07 · 12/36
steps.speakerNotes: With d equal to eight and a stride of two there are three windows: positions zero, two and four.

steps.label: KP07 · 12/36 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: With d equal to eight and a stride of two there are three windows: positions zero, two and four.

steps.label: KP07 · 12/36 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Cell seven: no window reads it.

steps.label: KP07 · 12/36 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: We round down because the kernel moves in whole steps and a leftover of less than one step is dropped. A common error: thinking the rounding is a minor detail. In fact it means cells at the right and bottom of the input may never be read.

steps.label: KP07 · 13/36
steps.speakerNotes: A stride larger than one has two side effects. First, the output gets smaller: for a 224 by 224 input, a three by three kernel, one ring of padding and a stride of two, the output side is 112, about one over s of the original.

steps.label: KP07 · 13/36 (1)

steps.label: KP07 · 13/36 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Second, KP06 showed that a convolution with stride s is equivariant only to shifts that are multiples of s.

steps.label: KP07 · 13/36 (3)

steps.label: KP07 · 14/36

steps.label: KP07 · 14/36 (1)

steps.label: KP07 · 14/36 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: The most common is zero padding; there are also constant padding and replicate padding.

steps.label: KP07 · 14/36 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: And reflect and circular padding. Five methods in all; let us look at them one by one.

steps.label: KP07 · 15/36
steps.speakerNotes: Zero padding: fill both ends with zero; the result is zero, three, one, four, two, zero.

steps.label: KP07 · 15/36 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Zero padding: fill both ends with zero; the result is zero, three, one, four, two, zero.

steps.label: KP07 · 15/36 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Constant padding: fill both ends with a given constant, for example nine; the result is nine, three, one, four, two, nine.

steps.label: KP07 · 15/36 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Zero is the simplest and most common; a constant can set a background value. Remember that zero padding creates an artificial dark ring at the border.

steps.label: KP07 · 16/36
steps.speakerNotes: Replicate: the left padded cell is the edge value three and the right one is the edge value two; the result is three, three, one, four, two, two.

steps.label: KP07 · 16/36 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Replicate: the left padded cell is the edge value three and the right one is the edge value two; the result is three, three, one, four, two, two.

steps.label: KP07 · 16/36 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Reflect: mirror about the edge; the left cell takes the inner one and the right cell the inner four; the result is one, three, one, four, two, four.

steps.label: KP07 · 16/36 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Circular: join head and tail; the left cell takes the last value two and the right cell the first value three; the result is two, three, one, four, two, three. With the same one ring, the three methods give different ends.

steps.label: KP07 · 17/36
steps.speakerNotes: How to choose? See whether the padded values look like a real image. Zero padding creates an artificial dark ring at the border.

steps.label: KP07 · 17/36 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: How to choose? See whether the padded values look like a real image. Zero padding creates an artificial dark ring at the border.

steps.label: KP07 · 17/36 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Replicate and reflect let the pattern at the border continue. Circular suits data whose ends really join, for example a wrap-around panorama.

steps.label: KP07 · 17/36 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: A constant can set a background value, such as mean brightness. The source lists common uses of each method; this note has not checked them one by one. Look at the nature of the data first; there is no single correct padding.

steps.label: KP07 · 18/36
steps.speakerNotes: How many rings does same need? Take a stride of one; the output side is d minus f plus two p plus one. Requiring it to equal d gives two p equals f minus one.

steps.label: KP07 · 18/36 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: How many rings does same need? Take a stride of one; the output side is d minus f plus two p plus one. Requiring it to equal d gives two p equals f minus one.

steps.label: KP07 · 18/36 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: So p equals f minus one, divided by two. For a three by three kernel, one ring.

steps.label: KP07 · 18/36 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: For a five by five kernel, two rings. With an odd kernel side and a stride of one, padding f minus one over two rings gives same.

steps.label: KP07 · 19/36

steps.label: KP07 · 19/36 (1)

steps.label: KP07 · 19/36 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: An even kernel is the same: f equal to four gives p equal to one point five, not a whole number of rings, so there is no exact same.

steps.label: KP07 · 19/36 (3)
